Yesterday I opened the kitchen drawer that sticks in damp weather and found a key labeled PEARS. The label was in my father's handwriting. He formed his capital R as if it had somewhere urgent to go.

We never had a pear tree. We had a plum tree that produced six plums in a good year, all at the height of a passing deer's mouth. I called my sister.

“Pears,” she said. “Of course.”

This is her way of buying time. I could hear her rinsing something.

“The cabinet at the old house,” she said finally. “Remember the glass doors? Remember how the handles looked like pears?”

They had looked like ordinary handles to me. But I remembered the sound of that cabinet opening, a little gulp where the varnish caught. Inside were birthday candles, playing cards, and a blue vase too narrow to wash properly. Our father kept the key because the left door swung open whenever a bus went past.

I thanked her and hung up. Outside, somebody was teaching a child to ride a bicycle. I heard running shoes slapping the pavement, then just the faint ticking of the wheels, then the shoes again.

I put the key back. I have been trying to own fewer things, with uneven results. Still, it seemed unfair to throw it away on the very afternoon it had managed, after twenty years in a drawer, to open something.

Next time my sister visits, I'll ask her to draw those handles from memory.
